utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon everybody. I was advised that there are preliminaries from both parties. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The first matter I would need to raise in -- well, there's two matters, one in open session, one in private. I think the other matter to which the Court alluded would also be raised in private, so let me go to the second matter first, the one that can be raised in open. I raised this with Mr. Robinson today. As the Court will recall, the redirect examination of the previous witness was abbreviated as a result of the understandable interest on all sides to conclude the witness's testimony by the end of the court week and also to allot as much time as possible for the actual cross-examination rather than redirect. For that reason, I raised with Mr. Robinson the possibility of submitting a very few documents that I would have submitted to the witness during the course of redirect examination. It constitutes a total of six documents. I inquired whether there was any objection in principle on the part of the Defence to this proposed admission. Mr. Robinson indicated there was not. It's in light of the circumstances and the fact that it was a limited number of documents rather than a massive, wholesale submission. I provided Mr. Robinson with a list of the proposed documents so he could review the specifics, but I simply wanted to bring that to the Court's attention at the earliest opportunity so you know that matter is being considered. Once Mr. Robinson has had an opportunity to review the documents and indicate his position on them specifically, I'll make the formal submission to the Chamber. The second matter, as I indicated would be in private session, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go into that, I wonder whether Mr. Robinson is in a position to give any confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I haven't had a chance to discuss the specific documents with Mr. Karadzic yet, so I can't say whether or not we would agree, but in principle we will try to co-operate and facilitate the admission of the exhibits, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, in the meantime, did the Chamber receive that list of documents yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I can do so, Your Honour, if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This deals with the 62 ter statement of the witness who is about to come in to testify, and we thought it would be better to deal with this before she came, rather than asking her to be excused when she had identified her 92 ter statement. There are some points in the statement that we ask to be excluded, and they relate to sniping and shelling incidents which are not charged in the indictment, in particular, in paragraphs 10, 16 through 18, and 37. There are mention of some incidents which do not appear in the Schedule F or G which list the shelling and sniping incidents in the indictment. And it's our position that when specific mention is made of specific victims and dates that those things should have been pled in the indictment and that it would frustrate the Trial Chamber's order under Rule 73 bis (D) if the Prosecution were allowed to add new incidents that were not the subject of the indictment. As you know, you requested them to reduce the number of incidents and they did that. They eliminated Schedule G(3), (16), (17) and (18) and sniping incident F(13), and we think if they're allowed to introduce evidence of things that were never even in the indictment that that would be frustrating the Chamber's ruling in which the Chamber indicated it was gravely concerned about the scope of the Prosecution's case and the potential effect it would have on the fair and expeditious conduct of the trial and administration of justice. And I'm quoting from the decision on the application of Rule 73 bis that you issued on the 9th of October, 2009. The second issue relates to paragraph 38 of the statement, and we believe that this should be excluded on the grounds of physician/patient privilege. The witness is repeating what a patient told her about her father, and I have to admit this is an issue that is not -- we have not been able to find any jurisprudence on at the ICTY or the ICTR as to whether a physician/patient privilege is even recognised by the Tribunal. But it is recognised in other international instruments as well as many local jurisdictions, and we feel it ought to be recognised in this Tribunal. So those four -- those four groupings of paragraphs, paragraph 10, 16 through 18, and 37 we ask be excluded on the grounds that those incidents should have been in the indictment if the evidence were to be led on them, and paragraph 38 as a communication that is covered by the physician/patient privilege. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are not objecting to the -- oh, when we -- you may deal with it when it comes, but do you have any say as to the diary that the witness kept?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We don't object to the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The -- that privilege you referred to can be invoked by the physician or nurse but only can be waived by the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that unless the patient waives it, the physician or nurse is not allowed to give evidence without a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether the accused has any right or authority to interfere with that privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he has no right to interfere with the privilege but the Chamber, I think, would have an obligation if it believes that the privilege exists to make sure that there's been a waiver before privilege is violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I just had the opportunity to take brief look at paragraph 38. Separate from the probative value it will have, if any, can we not view it as a kind of direct observation of what the witness saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's definitely an observation of what the witness heard, but that's the whole point of the privilege because it says I asked her about this and then it quotes what she said. So it's a communication between a patient and a nurse. So we think it's directly covered by the privilege. I agree the probative value is low, but I think this is an issue -- there are also physicians who are going to be testifying in the case, and so this is an issue that will come up again and perhaps this would be a good time to try to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Morrison has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you no doubt are very aware of the position in the United States. Bearing in mind that there's no direct jurisprudence in the Tribunal, we're going to obviously have to look for guidance outside the scope of the -- our inherent findings in previous cases. You would agree, I presume, that there is a difference between medical privilege and legal privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the legal privilege is attorney/client privilege, if you're referring to that specifically provided for in the ICTY statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And presumably in the US, as in the UK, that is a distinction which is recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is recognised. It's a different privilege, a privilege -- it's a stronger privilege for lawyer/client communication than it is for patient/physician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the privilege is one, that the President has said, that can be raised by the physician but only waived by the patient because it's the patient's privilege, as in a legal sense it would be the -- an accused's person privilege in an attorney/client relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But the difference surely is this: That where it's an issue of confidentiality, medical confidentiality, it's called privilege, but in reality it's an issue of confidentiality between the physician and the patient. If the doctor elects to ignore that privilege, that's not a matter for the Court. The issue then becomes an issue between the patient and the doctor or the doctor's, as it were, ethical obligations or medical council, or whatever, in the jurisdiction that that doctor practices rather than an issue for the Court. What the issue for the Court is whether or not what is likely to be said is relevant and probative and is generally of assistance in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the Court has to deal with whether the privilege -- whether it can hear evidence which is being offered in violation of the privilege. This actually came up in the Simic case with respect to the Red Cross. In that case, there was an employee of the International Red Cross who was ready willing and able to give evidence about what he had observed while working with the Red Cross and had given a statement to the Prosecution about those things. But the Chamber ruled that it was the privilege of the Red Cross that was at issue, and unless they waived that privilege, despite the willingness of the employee that it would exclude the evidence, and it did exclude the evidence, because the Red Cross wasn't willing to waive that privilege. So I think although the privilege should be invoked by the person who is appearing before the Chamber, we can't -- the Chamber has the right -- has the obligation to see that the privilege isn't violated and needs to have some evidence from the privilege holder that they've waived it, regardless of the willingness of the person who's here before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- as I say, that would be -- would not be the position in the UK law, and would not be the position, as I understand it, in the US law. The question of whether or not the Court would admit the evidence would be balancing exercise as to whether or not the breach of confidentiality was justified in the circumstances of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the UK and the US are a little different on that. The UK --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Robinson kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I've been asked to slow down. Sorry about that. I think my understanding is the UK looks at it as a policy issue, and the US and some other jurisdictions look at it more as a technical privilege issue. I have to say that in the US, it's only available in civil cases, not in criminal cases. But I believe in civil cases, when the privilege issue comes up, the US will not allow the evidence unless there's a waiver by the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But is that perhaps that the US is a far more litigious society?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We certainly are, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will it be Ms. Sutherland or Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, Mr. Robinson's objections to the admission of parts of Mrs. Zaimovic's statement, on the basis that it includes evidence of acts not charged in the indictment, is misguided on three fronts. First of all, her evidence is relevant to the charges of terror contained in the indictment. And passages of the paragraphs that Mr. Robinson referred to do contain that. It's also relevant to the allegations of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population of Sarajevo, which is contained in the indictment. And as Your Honours know, appellate jurisprudence allows for the admission of evidence related to unscheduled incidents as proof of general elements of the crimes charged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading for the interpretation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can go to the first point that her evidence is relevant to the charges of terror contained in the indictment. It requires the Prosecution to prove acts or threats resulting in grave consequences to the victim, and grave consequences include death or serious injury as well as psychological impact on the population. And that is to say, evidence of actual terrorisation may contribute to establishing other elements of the crime of terror; for instance, grave consequences. And that's the Dragomir Milosevic Appeals Chamber judgement of the 12th of November, 2009 at paragraphs 33 and 35. Her evidence is also relevant to the allegations of widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population and that's -- I take Your Honours to paragraph 88 of the indictment, and it's well established in the jurisprudence that they -- that the crimes against humanity require proof of the existence of a widespread or systematic attack on the civilian population. And that's Perisic Trial Chamber decision on the Prosecution's submission on interpretation of the Trial Chamber's decision of the 15th of May, 2007, regarding unscheduled incidents. The decision is dated the 31st of October, 2008, and it's at paragraph 11. That decision cites to Article 5 of the Tribunal in Blaskic Trial Chamber judgement of the 3rd of March, 2000, in paragraph 98. In fact, it's incorrect and this should be to the Appeals Chamber judgement of the 29th of July, 2004, paragraph 98. Mrs. Zaimovic's evidence is also relevant to the general nature of the shelling and sniping campaign directed against civilians, and the details provided by her in relation to the unscheduled incidents that Mr. Robinson refers to are integral to a necessary -- to evaluate her observations. In relation to the third point that the appellate jurisprudence allows for the admission of evidence related to unscheduled incidents as proof of general elements of the crimes charged, Galic Appeals Chamber judgement of the 30th of November, 2006, paragraph 219 states that evidence regarding additional incidents could be introduced at trial pursuant to Rule 93 of the Rules, in order to prove a consistent pattern of conduct relevant to the charges in the indictment, including a campaign. There's also the case of Seselj which we referred to in our OTP first Rule 73 bis submission. And that's the Seselj interlocutory appeal decision on appeal against the Trial Chamber's oral decision of 9 January 2008, and the decision's dated the 11th of March, 2008. At paragraph 24, where they affirm the Trial Chamber's ruling that evidence of crime sites removed under Rule 73 bis (D) can go towards proving the purposes and methods of a number of things which include the general elements of the persecution campaign. Your Honour, for those reasons, I submit that the evidence that Mr. Robinson wishes to have excluded from paragraphs 10, which discusses an attack -- sorry, a shelling that happened on the 14th of May, 2000 -- 1992, and the evidence at paragraphs 16 to 18 which deal with shellings which occurred at a school and in the Otoka area in November 1993, and in relation to the evidence he seeks to have excluded at paragraph 37 which relates to a shelling incidents which occurred on the 10th of October, 1992. With respect to the evidence at paragraph 38, which has been discussed between Mr. Robinson and the Bench already, the Prosecution -- it's the Prosecution's position that this should be dismissed for a number of reasons, the first being that Mr. Robinson has not established the existence of a physician/patient privilege, and the recognition of such a privilege would frustrate international criminal proceedings, and in any event, in our submission, the type of information at issue is not likely to be governed by a physician/patient privilege. If I can turn to the first bases that he hasn't established -- the Rules are obviously silent and that has -- we have been able to find no decision, either ICTY or ICTR that recognises the existence of this privilege under conventional customary international law. Rather, the approach consistent with Tribunal jurisprudence would be that where a third party confidentially exists, as Your Honours have already said, it's for the Trial Chamber who has the discretion to weigh it against the interests of justice, including the need to ensure that all relevant and probative evidence is available to the Chamber. The accused -- or Mr. Robinson, I should say, his general claim that a -- of a medical privilege would not further the objectives. Mr. Karadzic is subject to proceedings for having committed crimes against individuals, and, in our view, he shouldn't be permitted to assert the victim's physician/patient privilege as a bar to allowing relative and probative evidence. This Tribunal was established for the Prosecution of persons responsible for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. And it is, therefore, evident that either medical records or other evidentiary material connected with medical assistance may be of importance and to allow the Defence to assert the privilege to oppose the use of evidence could lead to the stultification of international criminal proceedings. Your Honour referred to the case of the United States jurisdiction, and it's our submission that even under US law, the fact of a patient stating this to, in fact, a nurse, as opposed to a physician would not be privileged even in the United States. For those reasons, Your Honour, I submit that all of the evidence that Mr. Robinson objects to should be allowed to remain in the amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the paras 10, 16 to 18 and 37, we agree with the observation given by Ms. Sutherland. They are relevant to the general facts regarding terrorising and chapeau and general requirements of the crime of the statute. As regards 38, while we do agree with the Prosecution's submission that in this case that patient and physician privilege is not subject -- is not to be applied in this case, we do not find that paragraph of great probative value; i.e., in order to be admitted as to the truth of the girl's belief that para (A) is too speculative or argumentative. So in that basis, we would not admit that paragraph, i.e., paragraph 38. So your objection is partly overruled and partly granted, Mr. Robinson. That said, shall we begin with our evidence. Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Fatima Zaimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I was advised that there's an outstanding motion of the addition of 65 ter list to two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there is no objection to it, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is granted. And I was also told there was remaining business from the previous witness, Exhibit 779 or 799. So if you could remind me of that matter later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Fatima Zaimovic is my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I will proceed with the requirements of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, on the 26th of February, 2010, you signed an amalgamated statement; is that correct? 2010, yes.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 22274 be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of page 1?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 13. Sorry, the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, you confirmed that this statement was read back to you in the Bosnian language. However, upon reviewing the statement yesterday, you wished to make a correction to one paragraph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 5 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The correction relates to paragraph 15, regarding the first sentence. The words "sniper fire" should read "shell-fire"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the two patients from the internal client that are referred to in that first sentence are the two patients referred to -- the same two patients referred to in paragraph 13 above?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just go to the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you wish to correct the statement by deleting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, where paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You wish to correct the statement by deleting the heading directly above paragraph 15 and the first three sentences of paragraph 15 which related to those two patients; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So do you confirm that with the above corrections, your amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked under oath about these topics today?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I seek to have the amalgamated witness statement 65 ter number 22274 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With the caveat of the paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no objection, but I would ask if the last sentence of paragraph 15 is being maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it whole para will be deleted. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the correction the witness wanted to make was in relation to the sniper fire. So it was simply the first three sentences which referred to the two patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said three sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm referring, myself, where she said: "From time to time, I found pieces of bullets and slugs in an attic room --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the fourth sentence. So we simply are asking for the first three sentences to be redacted and the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So you will produce a redacted version later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted as?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P814, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 814. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours leave, I'll now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. Mrs. Zaimovic has lived all of her life in Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1979, she became the head of nursing in the Children's Surgery Department of the Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo. She remained working in that position throughout the war, 1992 to 1995. During this time, Mrs. Zaimovic kept her own diary about the patients wounded during the war. She listed in her notes the names of 331 wounded children treated in the Children's Surgery Department of the Kosevo Hospital. Wounded children were also treated at the Sarajevo State Hospital, Dobrinja General Hospital, and the Orthopaedic Clinic and Traumatology Clinic. Mrs. Zaimovic describes in detail the consequences of the shelling and sniping on patients and staff and traumatisation suffered by the children. The Kosevo Hospital buildings were often shelled throughout the war, and a number of staff were killed as a result of shelling. The witness was working at the hospital when it was shelled, killing two patients and wounding another who were hospitalised in the nearby internal medicine clinic. Mrs. Zaimovic witnessed, on a regular basis, the tank shelling -- a tank shelling Sarajevo town from the area of Osmice in Serb-held territory. Mrs. Zaimovic describes treating patients from shellings which occurred at the Fatima Gunic school on 9 November 1993 and at Otoka on 10 November 1993. She also describes the burn injuries as a result of gas explosions. The witness describes the shortage of utilities and medical supplies and conditions under which she and her colleagues operated in the hospital during the war, in particular the problems related to the lack of electricity and sufficient water. Operating conditions were very difficult, especially in the winter. Mrs. Zaimovic also describes the personal sniping incidents and consequences of shelling and sniping on the witness and her family. The witness felt constant fear throughout the war, afraid for her family, and for the injured and wounded children. Your Honours, that concludes the brief summary of the witness’s evidence, and I now intend to question the witness for approximately 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And to highlight various aspects of her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, as your amalgamated witness statement is now in evidence in this case, I will be asking you only a limited number of questions relating to matters contained in your statement. Before I do that, I would like you to orient the Trial Chamber as to the location of the Kosevo Hospital on a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I would ask that 65 ter number 11791 be brought up onto the screen, please. Your Honours, this is a map of Sarajevo and its environs, and it's map 1 in the Sarajevo specific court binder which has been distributed to Your Honours and the accused and the parties.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Kosevo Hospital is close to the centre. If we look at the stadium, the sports stadium here, it's here roughly. That's where it is. Somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As Exhibit P815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I ask that 65 ter number 09390A be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, do you recognise what is marked in red directly below the word "Breka" on the map?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Right underneath that word is the entire complex -- or compound of the Kosevo Hospital. It's an enormous compound containing 36 large clinics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P816, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we still have that map on the screen, are you able to point to where the main entrance road is.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is here, around Bolnicka street. That's where the entrance would be. The hospital actually had two entrances, one the main entrance and the other one the back entrance, as it were. One was close to the orthopaedic clinic, right above the hospital itself. So those are the two entrances that existed. This was the main entrance, and this is where most of the ambulances entered the hospital premises. It's in this first part here where Bolnicka street is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And you -- your marking is where the -- the brown -- the line -- the road is marked in brown on the Bolnicka street side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that Rule 65 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that Rule 65 ter number 22797 be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, do you recognise what's shown in this satellite aerial image?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is the entire hospital compound. If you wish, I can point it out to you. It is this part around here. That's the compound of the hospital where I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you like the witness to mark the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can draw with a light pen.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: What is it that you would like me to point out?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The grounds of the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you also point to the location of the Children's Surgery Department during the war.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Children's Surgery Department was close to the main gate. These are three big Austrian buildings. That's it. We were in the first building here. That's where our department was. These buildings are linked by long corridors or halls. Also, the clinic of urology was there, pulmonology, the operation rooms, and so on. Neurosurgery was there as well, but it was moved to another area afterwards, but basically all the surgery departments were in this area, along with five operation rooms that were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't intend to tender a marked diagram, but for the -- for the record, the witness pointed to where the Children's Surgery Department was, and it's the -- the second building, the most southern -- south-eastern building on the -- on the image within the compound, the Kosevo Hospital compound, and it has a red tiled roof. I would seek to tender that document into -- that image into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As marked. As marked by the witness or without marking?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Without the marking, or if -- if -- if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we admit the marked version --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Marked version [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, if you could kindly sign your signature on that image and date of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If it's going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today's the 5th; right? Is it the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as we're going to admit a marked one, Your Honour, perhaps Mrs. Zaimovic could put a C where the Children's Surgery Department is. Just above the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the unannotated map will be Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think we need to admit the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The annotated map will be P817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I wish to now turn to matters contained in your statement. I have a number of questions related to the notes that you kept before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is mentioned in paragraph 9 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, you stated that you kept this personal diary regarding the patients wounded during the war who were treated in the Children's Surgery Department. How did you keep the diary? Was it -- was it a typed notes, handwritten notes? How was the -- how was the diary?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes when I'd have time, I'd type it out on a regular typewriter. There weren't any computers in our hospital at the time. Sometimes I'd write it in my own hand. You can see in the diary itself that the handwriting is sometimes a bit more nervous, looks scribbled. In addition to this diary that I kept as the head nurse, I also submitted regular reports that went to the administrative service, the administration of the hospital. This is something that was personal, for my very own point of view. It had to do with the very special situation involved when wounded children were brought into the hospital. Every one of these children had a story to tell, as it were, in view of that most unfortunate situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, I want to concentrate just on the questions in relation to the keeping of the diary. So the handwriting, whose handwriting was it, all of the handwritten entries, are they all your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the typed records?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you record the names of the patients?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I recorded patients names when they would be brought in, or perhaps a bit later when I'd have enough time in view of all the work I had then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the dates, are they all in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you kept the notes for your own -- you said it was something personal for your very own point of view. Did you -- did you list every wounded child? Did you manage to do that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, every wounded child, I think. Maybe there may be some that I omitted to -- to record, but for the most part it's all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What information did you generally record for each patient?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The name and surname of the child, the date when the child was admitted, the child's date of birth, the address of residence or the address from which the child had come, and the neighbourhood, the part of town that the child had come from. Also, the patient's diagnosis. The diagnosis was recorded by the doctors, of course. I would just copy it out from the other document. And also there would be date when the patient was discharged or died or was transferred to another clinic or was transferred to another country.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were the majority of injuries to the children sustained?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: All children that were brought in and that were recorded in this diary were injured by shrapnel or sniper fire. A very small number of children were also injured by phosphorous shells, those that cause burns, and some were injured by gas explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many wounded children were treated in the hospital in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, 163 children were brought to our clinic. Out of the 163, nine died at the clinic itself, but all the children that died on the spot were not brought to our clinic. They were brought to the morgue directly or to the mortuary where we sent our own patients who had passed away while in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter number 16843 be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: They are my impressions, the ones that I recorded and wrote down personally. My feelings, what I felt on that day, the day here being the 10th of October, 1992, what the situation was like around me and within me. It was something personal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, what is shown on page 2?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Page 2 shows the names and surnames of the patients who had gone outside the country, who were very seriously injured, and they were sent with the physicians of the world to be helped and treated further, because we were no longer able to do anything for them. We didn't have the necessary resources or equipment to deal with these extremely difficult cases, severely wounded children. And some of them left in 1992, some in 1993, and perhaps some children left later, which I might not have recorded in this list, but mostly these are children that went abroad for treatment. There were 32 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, just to note, this is page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Page 2 in English. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, can you describe very, very briefly what is on page 4 of the B/C/S and 3 of the English?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see the names of patients who were wounded on the 9th of September, 2002, their names, their date of birth, the type of injury they sustained and the day they were discharged. Here we have a little boy, his name was Sergije Bjelos, who was wounded in 1992 on the 14th of September, and his wounds were so severe that he died as a result of his injuries. There are quite a few more names. If you would like me to read them out, I will do so and I can say a few words about them. Of course, it's been a long time since then, so I might not remember them all, but most of them I do. All those children are constantly with me. I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, as we have only a limited amount of time, I want to take you to certain entries in this -- in this -- in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that we go to page 14 of the B/C/S and page 12 of the English please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, I draw your attention to entry which is numbered 210, Muamer Mrdic.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also entry number 212, Camo.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what do you want me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What -- what is the date that -- that the patients were treated?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Muamer Mrdic was admitted on the 1st of May, I think it was, as far as I can see here, 1993, and he was born on the 17th of February, 1974. The date of discharge is the 6th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic -- if I can interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we blow-up the B/C/S, please, so that you can see the date clearly. It's not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of May, 1993. He came from Dobrinja. And he had a very serious injury to his abdomen with his injuries to the colon, and so on, a rupture to the colon, and he was discharged in July 1993, but he came in in May, and he spent almost two months in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, do you see the date of the -- of the victim -- the patient, sorry, above Colic --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Colic. Esmeralda Colic, yes, I see that. The 31st of May, 2003 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, you have the original of your diary in front of you. Do you want to look at the original which is a better copy of, I think, what we have on the screen, just to check whether the date is in fact, the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness be given leave to refer to her -- to her original notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. But, Ms. Zaimovic, could you find Muamer Mrdic in the list. To me, his date of birth looks like 1st of June; is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just take a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of June, '06 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was the date that he was admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of June, 1993, yes, that's right. So this is a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 1st of June here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the date of birth, is that next to his name?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The date of birth is the 17th of February, 1979. The 17th of February, 1979.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in relation to Mrdic and also Camo, is the date -- sorry, for the date for Camo, is that also the 1st of June, 1993, as being the date admitted?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the 1st of June. Three children were admitted on that same day, the 1st of June. The 1st of June there, the 1st of June, and the 1st of June, including Camo, Samir. He came on the 1st of June, 1993, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: And he was born in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. Do you know in relation to number 210 and 212 the -- where they came from? I think you mentioned already that Mrdic came from Dobrinja. Do you know where Camo came from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Camo came from Petra Drepsin street, number 1. Now, where that street was, I can't tell you now. I really don't know, but that's the street name. I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Sutherland, I don't want to interrupt with these minor questions, but I found that the entry numbers are not matching between the English translation and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Samir Camo has no number, while Irfan Sehovic has 212, but if you look at original, Camo is numbered as 212.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Camo, Samir is 212, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that note, we shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I would now ask to go to page 30 in the B/C/S and 21 of the English -- I'm sorry. Before we do that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, could you just give a very brief description of the injuries of Mrdic and Camo.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mrdic, Muamer had an injury to the abdomen and a fracture of the femur due to a shell explosion, and he sustained several types of injury, in fact. Camo, Samir had head injuries and the femur of the fracture and the upper leg, and those are the type of injuries that people sustain when a shell explodes. They have multiple injuries, not just one but multiple injuries, and these children came in that way, injuries caused by shells exploding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'll move on to another entry, page 30 of the B/C/S and page 21 of the English, please. Mrs. Zaimovic, I ask you to look at entry number 291. What was the date this patient was treated? First of all, the patient's name.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean, Kapetanovic, Muhamed Kapetanovic? Is that the one? 291, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. What date was he treated?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He arrived on the 22nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where he was brought from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He arrived from Alipasino Polje. And in my diary, I recorded that six other children died -- were killed together with him, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Zaimovic, I'm looking at the English translation. Amina Birdzo, that also entry 291 in the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 292 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is Amina Birdzo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a girl. She was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: 292. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now go to another entry on page 31 of the B/C/S and page 22 of the English. Mrs. Zaimovic, I ask you to look at entry number 294.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The name of that patient is Sabahudin --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sabahudin, Ljusa, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] patient?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Born in 1983 and came to the clinic on the 4th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where this patient was brought from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: From Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That reference to 3 Oslobodilaca Sarajevo street, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the street he lived in. That's the street he lived in. The name of the street. Sarajevo has, of course, different street names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the next entry, number 295. What date was this patient treated and the name of the patient?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: This patient was admitted on the 5th of February, 1994. Denis Stuhlik, born in 1979. Ilija Grbic street is where he lived in Sarajevo, and he was injured at the marketplace of Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to page 32 of the B/C/S but still page 22 of the English. Mrs. Zaimovic, if you look at entry number 296.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the name of this patient?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Nejla Basic, born in 1991, also wounded at Markale market. On the same date, the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I can turn to page 33 of the B/C/S, still on page 22 of the English. I'm sorry, if you look at the next entry, number 297. I'm sorry. Could you -- could you --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The 5th of February, 1994, that's when she was admitted. Enesa Daidzic. Enesa, mother of the child, born in 1952. That's the mother of the child. And we have her child, too, also -- she and her child were wounded at the marketplace, but they recovered from their wounds. They weren't killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what does it say in the second column in relation to their injuries?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The mother had wounds from explosives in -- injured in her leg and in the thorax. And the child had an injury above her knee from the shells. The shrapnels from shells hit them and wounded them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 33 of the B/C/S and still on page 22 of the English and is that entry number 298?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again does it say this is in relation to Aldijan Daidzic. Does it say where he came from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Aldijan Daidzic, yes. On the 5th of February, 1994, was when he was admitted together with his mother. Sutjeska street, Sarajevo, was the address. That's where they both lived. You see that Sutjeska street is recorded for the mother and child. And it says in brackets that the mother and child were together. They had both undergone a great shock so you couldn't separate the mother and the child.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour I seek to tender 65 ter 16843 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter number 22798 be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, how much longer do you have with this witness? Because I'm seeing the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Maybe five, ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These entries are taking a little bit longer than I anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, do you recognise that document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean from number 1 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, if -- if -- if --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this -- is this list also part of your diary?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is -- this is actually the beginning of the diary as opposed to the last document we saw which started with patient number 98, I think; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the beginning. This is when the children first arrived in our clinic. The first child was Emir Zolj and then further down the list, and the injuries became more and more severe as you go down the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, with this document here, if -- if -- these were -- these were pages that you produced to the Office of the Prosecutor at a different time to the -- to the first lot of pages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the Prosecutor took what he considered necessary, and I think you did the same. You took what you felt you needed, and among those documents is this first page, and I'm happy to see that you took that page because these were very seriously injured children. For us in the health sector, the injuries were shocking. A little girl suffered from paraplegia. There were very serious injuries which we had never seen before, the likes of which we'd never seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, if we can just bring up -- back Exhibit P818, please. Quickly.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment. And if we could go to the -- once the document comes up. The last exhibit, the one that -- just page 1. Page 1. And then if you could go to the very end page. Page 35 in the B/C/S and page 23 in the English. Mrs. Zaimovic, you see that this last number in this document goes up to number 307. If you look at the screen --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm looking for it. Just let me take a moment, please. Here it is, yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the beginning of these patients, if we can go back to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Page 3 of the English - I'm sorry - starts on patient 99. You agree?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can -- if we can now bring back onto the screen the document we just had, and that was document number 22798. Mrs. Zaimovic, were you asked to provide the list of the patients either side of patients number 99 to 307 the other day, so patients numbered 1 to -- to 98, and then patients 308 to 331?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in relation to that, when you provided the -- the additional pages this year, you said that there was some changing in numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers were corrected a long time ago. When we saw that mistakes had been made, they were corrected and aligned with the number of children, and that's quite normal. You know, when you're writing under a situation of that kind, which was a terrible time, you tend to make a mistake in the number of children. It's not the number that's important. What is important is just how many children were killed and how many children were wounded. That is the most important thing in all this. And it's terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the numbers --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You ought to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the numbers changed, correct me if I'm wrong, because there were some handwritten entries within the typed pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, why was that changed? Well, I realised that I had omitted to list some of the children because I had a lot of work to do. I was very busy and I was under a lot of stress. And then when I remembered, I would add them in and correct the numbers, and you can see that for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to page 16 of the B/C/S of this document and page 14 of the English. If I can ask you to look at entry numbered 308.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this patient was admitted?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: This patient was admitted on the 24th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How old is this patient?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Drazen Gelo, and he was born on the 10th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where he was brought from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The street that he was brought from was called Safeta Zajke number 88. His father's name was Ivan, and the wound he sustained was from an explosive device, from an explosion, and part of the shell, the shrapnel and metal remained lodged in his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask to go to page 23 of the B/C/S and page 18 of the English. And I draw your attention to number 328. When was this patient admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Andreja Svoboda was the name, admitted on the 28th of August, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how old --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: -- from Sarajevo. The girl was born on the 22nd of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know where she was brought from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: From Sarajevo. The street name was Darovalaca Krvi number 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit Number P819.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know when you wanted to take the break, and I know that I have taken a lot longer than half an hour in relation to these diary entries, but I would ask for your indulgence for another ten minutes, five to ten minutes with this witness. I have another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- six questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, in your statement at paragraph 36, you say mention that children were very frightened and traumatised. Can you describe briefly for the Court the children's reactions to the sniping and the shelling?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: All the children who came to our clinic were traumatised, first of all, because of the injuries they had sustained. After that, they were hospitalised. Shelling went on in town, and whenever a shell fell, they would jump out of bed. They were traumatised. They were afraid. Some of them peed in their beds. They were terrified. They asked the nurses to protect them, to help them. It was very hard to deal with them. It was very hard to carry out medical interventions. So this war trauma was more than visible in that period on all the children. It was particularly difficult when we had to move the children into basements, halls, in such conditions and it was simply substandard, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did this occur when you were having to take children to the basement?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it depended on the shelling. Children would be taken out in the middle of the day, in the middle of the night. The heavier the shelling, the more likely it was. Then we would be instructed to take the children to shelters, basements as quickly as possible. That was the only way in which we could help them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this happening on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the psychological impact on the children as a result of the sniping and the shelling that you were -- that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distinguished Ms. Sutherland is putting many leading questions, and she is putting questions to the witness as if she were a psychiatrist or an expert. She's a witness here. She's not a psychiatrist. And now she is dealing with certain matters that are not for this witness to speak about. Perhaps somebody else could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mrs. Zaimovic, it's for the Chamber. Mr. Karadzic, what she asked is the symptom or the phenomenon as she witnessed or observed. As such, there's -- there's nothing the witness should be prohibited from saying anything. The objection is overruled. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: After the shelling, the children -- a great many children started wetting their beds. Before that, they hadn't done that. When a shell would be fired, they would start screaming so hard, and they'd flee to the nurses, asking them for protection. That is truly what happened at the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said the shells would be fired, where would -- what would they be fired on?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Shells were falling all over the place. They were shooting at will. Whatever -- they did whatever they wanted to do. They shelled apartments, buildings, marketplaces, wherever. Whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often -- I'll rephrase the question. How -- was -- you mentioned in your statement that the hospital was shelled on a number of occasions. What was the result of -- of the shelling in relation to the actual Children's Surgery Department building?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Our building was shelled. It's a big building built in the Austrian times. It has enormous windows, and all of the windows were broken. There was no glass on any of the windows. Can you imagine what it's like to work under these conditions in such rooms?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you witness -- in relation to the children, did you witness any other impacts on them as a result of the shelling and the sniping? You mentioned that the children were wetting the bed.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: They were frightened always. Whenever they'd hear anything loud, they would jump out of bed. They were drawing things because we tried to calm them down in that way. Whatever they drew was a reflection of the war. You could not see a child draw a pretty picture. All of them had to do with the war, burning, shelling, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the shelling and the sniping that -- that you were involved in. What effect did -- did the shelling of your residential building, which you mentioned in paragraph 43 of your statement, what effect did that have on you and your family?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Our building was shelled often like all other buildings. As for my own apartment, a shell fell in the bedroom. Thankfully we weren't there at the time. But, indeed, we were all frightened. Believe me, the entire family was frightened. Whenever you'd go to the hospital or wherever, you didn't dare look. Somehow you'd keep your head down, and you'd be thinking that your turn had come, that you'd be the victim of such a shell or of a sniper. I was terribly frightened. I have to tell you that in all sincerity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what psychological or physical injuries do you suffer from today as a result of the shelling and sniping which occurred in Sarajevo in 1992 and -- between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Not sniper or shelling, but once, when my husband and I had set out to work, someone had aimed at us with a sniper. Thankfully we were not hit. It was near the entrance to the orthopaedics clinic. Somehow the sniper fired between myself and my husband, and then we decided not to go to work together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. And a redacted version of the witness's statement, Exhibit P814, has been uploaded with the redactions to paragraphs 15 and 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I omitted to say that the previous question that I was referring to, whether it was a regular thing, et cetera, in my view that was a leading question, but let it be. Cross-examination by Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Zaimovic.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic, and I'm glad to see you here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm glad to see you as well. Tell me, please, when did you come from Mitrovica to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a three-month-old baby.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I see. Is this your maiden name?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, my maiden name is Arifovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. What does your husband do?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: My husband is a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was he before that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he do something in the meantime. I mean, what was his education? Did he complete any kind of school?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He completed a secondary medical school. I think he socialised with you and some other people from that school, and then he entered university and then got a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to ask you about, because I'd be surprised if he hadn't told you that we had been friends.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He did tell me that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear that in mind, that since you are speaking the same language, please put a pause between question and answers. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you lived at Breka, which street?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Susic is the name of my street, and it's number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We knew Hasan Susic as well, didn't we? Tell me, when did you move there?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We moved there in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You moved to that apartment, you mean?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you go to work? Did you walk or did you take the car?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We walked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What street or through which streets?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the area?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We'd just go down by one building, we'd go through the passage and then we'd enter the orthopaedics clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the second row of houses at Breka; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So where did they fire at you with a sniper?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the steps between the entrance and the entrance into the orthopaedics clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is it true that your department for children's orthopaedics is the best hospital for that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the best hospital, but it's actually the best clinic, too. Were children treated elsewhere as well?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were children treated elsewhere as well, I mean, by surgeons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know what the town was like -- or, rather, you don't know because you were shooting from up there. Children were being treated at the state hospital, in Dobrinska Hospital. Some came to the orthopaedics department and some also came to the traumatology department, but most children were brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you become head nurse?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I became head nurse in 1979.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm a bit perplexed by something here. It says that that's what you did from September 1992 until August 1994. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said in your statement of the 18th of January, 2002, in the Galic case. The page is 1843. Namely, that you held that position between September 1992, and August 1994. Is this a new position?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's no position. I became the head nurse of the clinic in 1979, and that's what I did up until my retirement. I retired three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't understand why it says here that you worked from September 1992 until August 1994 at that position.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any changes in your position, in your professional position in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing was that I was an assistant at the higher medical school, and I worked as a teacher at the secondary medical school in addition to the regular work that I did, because my students would come to the clinic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This remains unclear. Tell me, you knew all the doctors in that compound quite well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, I knew my own doctors, the ones that I worked with, and the surgeons for the most part. At some of the other clinics, I knew most of the doctors, but you cannot really know everyone. You know how big the clinical centre is. You cannot really know everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have to wait. This street that you referred to, Bolnicka, is that the former street called Mose Pijade?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was always called Bolnicka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When I lived there, it was called Mosa Pijade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Bolnicka 25, well perhaps your part down this was called maybe Mosa Pijade, but this was called Bolnicka 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I guess that Mosa did something wrong because the whole street used to be called Mosa Pijade. Do you know why it was changed?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably because all streets in Sarajevo changed their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you knew professor Borisa Starovic, Professor Jovo Vranic, Professor Milutin Najdanovic, Andrija Gvozdenovic, Nemanja Veljkov.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also knew -- well, we have to wait for the interpretation. You knew Milica Lopandic as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement here, the one from the 9th of April, 2000, that is, on page 00938863, paragraph 3 -- actually, before that as well. In the amalgamated statement of the 26th of February, in paragraph 3, you say that before the outbreak of the war, some of the Serbs had left the hospital. Can you shed more light on that? When did they start leaving the hospital and why?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs left the hospital for the most part when the war started. Some Serbs like Andrija Gvozdenovic, your friend, got ill all of a sudden, sprained his ankle. What an excuse. And then he did not work in hospital for at least five or six months. From time to time he would come to see us. And on the basis of his views and his statements, we could realise that something was in the making, that something was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, so they hadn't left before the war, but when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then the statement should be corrected. Isn't that right? Isn't that right? Shouldn't the statement be corrected? It's not that they left before the outbreak of the war but when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: They left when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Further on you stay in your statement dated the 9th of April, 2000, 0038863, paragraph 4, that's the reference, that most of the Serbs and Croats who were doctors stayed on, but they slowly started leaving one by one; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then you said on the 18th of January, 2002, transcript reference -- rather is the Galic transcript, IT-282 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. Fifteen nurses left, and two Croat women and three Serb women stayed there and continued working.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Until when did they work at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that it was two Croat women and three Serb women that stayed at work?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Croat women who had stayed on still worked there. They were young nurses. One of the Serb nurses was pensioned off and she left, and the other one left too. So, indeed, they were with us all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. What about some of the doctors who happened to be at their weekend cottages when the war broke out? Did they try to come back? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Professor Mirko Sosic, for example. He stayed on for a while and tried to work, right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did work. I don't know whether he had returned from his weekend cottage. I don't know about that. I just know that he returned, that he started working, and then he and his wife left the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this sound accurate to you, namely that Sarajevo was left by almost 250 doctors, physicians, primarily Professors Starovic; Sucur; Radivojevic; Kaufer, Leopold Kaufer; Guzina; Dusan Vukatic [phoen]; Marko Vukovic, and so on?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
