utterances.text: Well, that's a matter of politics, but that man really did work for quite a long time at our clinic, and he's still alive working in Belgrade. We met him recently, and when his wife gave birth to their son, we tried to help them out as best we could, taking them clothes and food and firewood, and so on. We never distinguished between anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, do you know that Enko Rustempasic was never forgiven - he was a Muslim doctor and his wife, Sonja Sorajic, a good anaesthesiologist, perhaps the best - for having contracted a mixed marriage, ethnically speaking, and when Sonja addressed the authorities for help, they wouldn't, and they said that they had to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think all that is pure invention, and that's the kind of rumour that was put about and led people to hate each other. That's what you keep doing all the time. You want to intensify hatred among people by putting out rumours of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, in due course, we'll provide evidence about that. Now, do you know about this man Kinez, who was the head of security at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of him, but I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But what was he, the head of what?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was at all, but I did hear his name mentioned, but I, myself, never met him, nor do I know him at all. Nor do I know that he was at the hospital either. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very well. We'll ask the Trial Chamber to show the statements of these people that you say I'm making them all up. Now, from the traumatology department were mortars fired around Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that's not true, and I don't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you say you know that it's not true.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's certainly not true, but I don't know. I'm sure people would have seen that, but I think that you're making it all up, big time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we both knew Dr. Milica Lopandic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and I liked her very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: She was Sreten Lopandic's wife; right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And they had a rather large apartment, very nice one?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what happened to Dr. Milica Lopandic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Does the Trial Chamber really want me to say what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I say that she was thrown out of the window because other people coveted her apartment?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You are lying. She wasn't thrown out. She was at our clinic all the time. We helped her. We brought her food. We visited her husband and all the rest of it. But because of the shelling, and she was terribly afraid of the shelling, she would frequently come to our basement where we would take refuge with our children, and she spent a lot of time there because she was very afraid of the shelling. And one day we heard that she had committed suicide jumping out of the window. Now, about this coveting of her apartment and seizing her apartment, that's just not true, but that can be investigated to see who actually did take her apartment. But Dr. Milica Lopandic merited every respect, but she suffered a nervous breakdown because of the tireless and ceaseless shelling in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when did Mrs. Lopandic die?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I don't know when she died, but we buried her, gave her a nice funeral. We waited for her daughter to arrive from America and her son from Belgrade, and we -- the clinical centre paid for the funeral. Professor Kolihagic [phoen] and Professor Dizdarevic, we all attended the funeral, regardless of the fact that there was shelling going on all the time. We all attended her funeral. And I think you're telling it a lot of lies, and I find it horrific to have to listen to everything you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I find it horrific too. I'm not saying that you threw her out of the window.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody threw her out of the window, and that's quite definite.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We're going to show what your big-time journalists write about this custom of throwing people out of windows. We'll come to that tomorrow. Do you maintain that people weren't thrown out of the window in order to kill them? And a Serbian poet said he didn't jump, they jumped him.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say, sir. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you say that the Sabotage Company of the 105th Brigade did not have a post at the bakery?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say that I don't know where this bakery was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where Juval Nitrak street was?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to a document now -- well, actually, we haven't called it up yet. But anyway, let's see what the reports were like about the situation in Kosevo Hospital, the supplies, and so on. And that, I think, is 948, document 948.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 948 called up on e-court, please. I think there's a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the translation, Mr. Karadzic -- I was told that there's none. You will have spent, by the end of today for your cross-examination, about two hours. Originally you indicated -- you projected your cross-examination to be four hours, and then later on you requested further -- more two hours. I'm speaking for myself, but I think you could conclude what you put today to the witness in less than half an hour or even 15 minutes. So discuss the way how to cross-examine with your legal advisor, and we expect you to conclude your cross-examination by the first session tomorrow. We have five more minutes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't think that will be sufficient, but in view of the allegations made by the witness, by the by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But let's focus on paragraph 3. This is a strictly confidential secret document. It says: "The Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo is well supplied with medicines, medical material, and sufficient quantities of blood. About 7.000 meals are served and prepared each day for the duty staff of which there are 1.200 and for about 1.500 patients. The meals are mostly made up the rice, beans, and macaroni. And in every fourth building of this institution, there's a separate place for worship, something like a mosque. The hospital is regularly supplied with gas, electricity, and water, and it also has gas-powered generators should the electricity supply be cut. The generators are maintained by UN members." What do you have to say to this report?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I can say is at the beginning of the war, when you cut off our electricity and water supply, the situation in the hospital was extremely difficult. We had no water and no electricity, and electricity was the main problem. Well, so was the water, and all the sheets that we used were destroyed because we had to use some very strong disinfectants, since we couldn't wash and launder clothes properly. So a lot of what it says here is not true. There was food, but of very poor nutritional value. We appealed to the citizens to bring in food to the children and pyjamas, sheets, and so on. That didn't happen until the physicians of the world turned up and UNICEF, and they helped us a lot to have the minimum supplies of food and medicines and sheets and everything else we needed in the hospital, but our situation was very difficult. We just had small weak lamps until the physicians of the world came in and brought in better equipment, together with UNPROFOR, to provide what the generators needed so that the operating theatres could function. So you're not being honest and sincere, Mr. Karadzic, to put out untruths like that to the -- you destroyed the city that provided you with your education and your life. Why don't you repent and tell the truth before this Trial Chamber? You destroyed thousands of people and lives. Your people, our people, our ethnicities, you destroyed everyone. And it's not fair of you. What you're saying now, you're not being fair. You're speaking and uttering terrible untruths. I apologise for my emotions, but this is something that I feel strongly about and that affects me deeply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, I am reading reports put out by intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: What intelligence services? You had spies everywhere. They were your intelligence services. What you did to us is terrible. You destroyed thousands of lives and people. So repent. Say it, I did that with my army. I did those things. But you don't want to do that. You don't want to say that. And you did do that. That's what you did. You killed innocent people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam -- the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know who was guilty, guilty. It was the writers of the Islamic Declaration. Those are the culprits. They were the culprits, as far as you were concerned, and as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I told you, we will not admit this document. Bear in mind, we will give you the first session tomorrow. We will rise for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of May, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.
